paper_title: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Memory has become integral to the LLM agent ecosystem, supporting information retention and reuse across interactions. However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory in a query-agnostic manner, which can incur unnecessary preprocessing cost and discard details that later prove essential. Recent studies have begun shifting memory processing toward runtime adaptation, but typically specialize in particular operations or fixed processing schemes, leaving flexible control over performance, cost, and latency largely underexplored. To address this challenge, we present \textbf{MemPilot}, a flexible framework that orchestrates on-demand memory curation under different performance--cost--latency preferences. Specifically, we optimize a multi-step LLM policy via reinforcement learning to iteratively choose between retrieving from query-agnostic memory and delegating query-specific curation of raw multimodal history to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. The policy jointly controls evidence amount, curation instructions, model selection, and visual access, enabling fine-grained allocation of runtime computation. To optimize this policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling by separately estimating each objective's advantage before aggregation. Moreover, we introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment across multi-step rollouts. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance--cost--latency trade-offs across optimization preferences, with preference sweeps yielding broader frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines.

Introduction As large language model (LLM) agents evolve toward persistent, long-horizon interaction, memory becomes increasingly central to preserving and reusing past experience (Hu et al., 2025; Huang et al., 2026). However, most existing agent memory systems construct memory from interaction histories in query-agnostic manner, and relying solely on such pre-query construction can be wasteful and lossy, as it cannot reliably anticipate future query needs (Fang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025). To mitigate this limitation, growing line of work moves memory adaptation to runtime through query-time evidence distillation, on-demand memory construction, and adaptive memory strategies (Yan et al., 2025a; Zhang et al., 2026d). Despite this progress, flexible orchestration of runtime memory adaptation remains underexplored, particularly when adapting runtime computation to query needs and multimodal evidence while balancing performance, cost, and latency (Zhang et al., 2026b). This raises key challenge: how can runtime multimodal memory curation be adaptively orchestrated with controllable performancecostlatency trade-offs? Unfortunately, addressing this challenge is non-trivial due to three key limitations of existing approaches to runtime memory adaptation. 1 Runtime memory control remains structurally rigid: existing methods typically rely on hand-designed operations or fixed processing pipelines, with efficiency Corresponding author(s): wazhz14@gmail.com MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents control hard-wired into predefined modules, budget tiers, or heuristics (Yin and Tang, 2026; Yu et al., 2026a; Zhang et al., 2026b), leaving few degrees of freedom for query-specific adaptation and making fine-grained trade-off optimization difficult. 2 Trade-off optimization remains incomplete: existing approaches often target only subset of efficiency objectives, such as token usage or monetary cost, while user-facing latency is rarely treated as an explicit optimization objective (Liu et al., 2026b; Zhang et al., 2026d). 3 Existing methods largely assume fixed processing backend for runtime memory adaptation, overlooking substantial variation in curation quality, cost, and latency across heterogeneous models and limiting adaptation to query difficulty and evidence modality, thereby constraining the achievable trade-off space (Yan et al., 2025a; Yu et al., 2026a). Collectively, these limitations call for more flexible framework that can orchestrate runtime memory operations and processing backends according to both query needs and optimization preferences. Building on these observations, in this work we introduce MemPilot, flexible framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under different performancecostlatency preferences. At high level, MemPilot follows simple design principle: retain query-agnostic memory, compatible with off-the-shelf agent memory systems, for efficient access, while preserving raw interaction history for query-specific runtime curation. Specifically, at inference time, multi-step LLM policy constructs query-adaptive orchestration trajectory by iteratively choosing between retrieving from the queryagnostic memory bank and delegating curation of the raw history to heterogeneous LLMs and vision-language models (VLMs), whose distinct capabilities naturally offer different quality, cost, and latency profiles. Rather than relying on hand-crafted pipelines or discrete budget tiers, the policy adaptively determines how much evidence to process, how it should be curated, which model to invoke, and whether visual evidences are needed, exposing fine-grained controls over runtime computation trade-offs. We optimize this policy with reinforcement learning under different performance, cost, and latency preferences. To better handle the resulting multi-objective optimization, we adapt objectivewise advantage decoupling by estimating each objectives advantage separately before weighted aggregation. We further introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation, which estimates the marginal contribution of individual curation steps for fine-grained credit assignment. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks show that MemPilot achieves favorable performancecostlatency trade-offs across different optimization preferences. Fine-grained preference sweeps further reveal broader trade-off frontiers than existing trade-off-aware baselines, while behavioral analyses show that MemPilot adaptively reallocates runtime computation as optimization preferences change. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce MemPilot, systematic framework for preference-aware runtime memory orchestration that jointly controls memory access, query-specific curation, heterogeneous model delegation, and visual evidence usage. By unifying these decisions within multi-step policy, MemPilot enables fine-grained performancecostlatency control without relying on fixed processing pipelines, predefined budget tiers, or fixed processing backend. To optimize the orchestration policy under competing objectives, we adapt objective-wise advantage decoupling and introduce prefix-based marginal utility estimation for fine-grained credit assignment in multi-step rollouts, enabling stable and effective optimization. Experiments on five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate favorable performance costlatency frontiers across preferences, with analyses revealing shifts in model selection, visual access, and computation allocation as preferences change. 2. Related Work 2 MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents 2.1. Agent Memory and Runtime Adaptation LLM agents increasingly rely on memory mechanisms to preserve and reuse information from longterm interaction histories (Packer et al., 2023; Zhong et al., 2024). Most existing text-centric systems construct memory before future queries are known, using either hand-designed mechanisms for extraction and organization (Chhikara et al., 2025; Fang et al., 2025; Kang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2025) or learned policies for memory construction, updating, and retrieval (Wang et al., 2025; Yan et al., 2025b; Yu et al., 2026b; Yue et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026a). Beyond text-centric memory, recent work has extended agent memory to multimodal interactions, maintaining structured representations over textual, visual, and other sensory experiences (Feng et al., 2026a; Liu et al., 2026b, 2025; Long et al., 2026; Wang and Chen, 2025). Despite increasingly adaptive and multimodal memory designs, they still construct memory in largely query-agnostic manner. growing line of work instead shifts memory processing toward runtime adaptation. GAM (Yan et al., 2025a) performs just-in-time research over stored memory and raw history, while BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b) learns query-aware runtime extraction under different computation budgets. MemGen (Zhang et al., 2025a) and AdaMEM (Zhang et al., 2026d) dynamically generate or refresh memory guidance according to evolving reasoning states, whereas MemRL (Zhang et al., 2026c) adapts the utility of stored experiences from interaction feedback. More recent work further explores query-time evidence distillation and deferred memory construction (Yin and Tang, 2026; Yu et al., 2026a). However, these approaches typically specialize in particular form of runtime adaptation or follow predefined processing pattern. MemPilot instead learns to orchestrate heterogeneous multimodal memory curation at runtime under controllable performancecostlatency preferences. 2.2. LLM Routing LLM routing aims to match different queries with suitable models based on their heterogeneous capabilities and costs. Early approaches route queries through model cascades or select models based on estimated query difficulty (Chen et al., 2023; Ding et al., 2024). More recent work improves routing through preference learning (Ong et al., 2025), contrastive objectives (Chen et al., 2024), and graphbased modeling (Feng et al., 2024), while further extending routing to multi-agent settings (Yue et al., 2025) and unified routing frameworks (Feng et al., 2026b). Moving beyond one-shot routing, several methods employ reinforcement learning to enable multi-step model selection and orchestration (Feng et al., 2026c; Qian et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2025b). These advances highlight the potential of LLM routing as general paradigm for adaptively allocating heterogeneous model computation according to task demands and resource constraints. 3. Methodology In this section, we first formulate on-demand memory orchestration as multi-step decision process (Section 3.1). We then instantiate the factorized curation and delegation decisions that enable query-adaptive runtime control (Section 3.2). Finally, we introduce resource-aware reward modeling for optimizing qualitycostlatency trade-offs with fine-grained credit assignment (Section 3.3). 3.1. On-Demand Memory Orchestration as Multi-Step Decision Process Dual-view memory representation. To support flexible runtime adaptation while retaining efficient access to query-agnostic memory, MemPilot maintains two complementary views of the interaction history: query-agnostic memory bank and the raw multimodal history . Factorized Memory Curation and Delegation Factorized curation controls. We next instantiate the structured action arguments 𝜙𝑡 to expose fine-grained control over runtime memory curation. Rather than relying on fixed processing pipeline or predefined budget tiers, MemPilot factorizes each action into several controllable dimensions, allowing the orchestrator to adapt what evidence to retrieve, how much to retrieve, how it should be curated, which model should process it, and whether visual evidence is needed. These decisions jointly provide flexible control over runtime computation and its resulting qualitycostlatency trade-offs. Heterogeneous model delegation. Beyond deciding what evidence to retrieve and how to curate it, MemPilot also adapts which model performs the runtime curation, since heterogeneous models exhibit distinct capabilities, monetary costs, and latencies, making model choice natural and effective control dimension for runtime trade-offs. Inspired by the LLM routing paradigm (Feng et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025b), MemPilot therefore delegates runtime curation to configurable pool of LLMs and VLMs, allowing the orchestrator to adaptively select model for each curation step under different optimization preferences. To support this routing decision, the orchestrator is given anonymized model IDs together with lightweight profiles describing key characteristics such as parameter scale and supported input modalities. The selected model 𝑚𝑡 then processes the retrieved evidence according to 𝑖𝑡 and returns textual observation to the orchestrator. For vision-capable routes, 𝑣𝑡 further determines whether raw images should be included in the curation request. Together, these factorized decisions allow each query to induce its own curation trajectory over evidence depth, processing strategy, model capacity, and modality access, providing flexible trade-off control without requiring rigid processing pipeline or predefined budget tiers. 5 MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents 3.3. We mainly evaluate MemPilot in multimodal settings involving both textual and visual interaction histories. Specifically, we use five multimodal agent-memory benchmarks: Mem-Gallery (Bei et al., 2026), WorldMemArena (Liu et al., 2026a), H2HMem (Zhu et al., 2026), MemEye (Guo et al., 2026), and MemLens (Ren et al., 2026), with MemEye and MemLens further serving as out-of-distribution evaluation sets. We evaluate answer quality using F1 score and an LLM-judge score (L-J), with GPT-4o-mini as the judge model. Cost measures the total token-based monetary cost incurred by both the orchestrator and delegated external models. Latency measures their total inference latency in seconds. Appendix A.1 and A.4 provide further details. Baselines. We organize baselines into two groups according to whether they support explicit trade-off control. The first group contains fixed-configuration methods used for the main comparison. It includes (1) text-centric memory systems including A-MEM (Xu et al., 2025) and SimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026c), (2) training-based memory methods including GAM (Yan et al., 2025a), AgeMem (Yu et al., 2026b), and Mem-T (Yue et al., 2026), and (3) multimodal memory systems including MIRIX (Wang and Chen, 2025), MemVerse (Liu et al., 2025), and M2A (Feng et al., 2026a). The second group contains (4) methods that explicitly expose performanceefficiency trade-offs, including LightMem (Fang et al., 2025), BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b), and OmniSimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026b). Section 4.4 compares these methods separately through frontier analysis. 4.2. Implementation Details MemPilot is implemented based on VeRL1, with Qwen3-4B-Instruct (Yang et al., 2025) as the default orchestrator policy. To disentangle gains from RL-enhanced answer generation, we additionally report decoupled-answer evaluation where the curated context is passed to separate, non-RL-trained answer model, using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct and Qwen3.5-9B. External LLMs and VLMs are accessed through OpenRouter2, with the heterogeneous model pool specified in Appendix A.2. We segment raw interaction histories into 256-token chunks and use Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025c) for semantic retrieval. Unless otherwise specified, the query-agnostic memory bank is constructed with LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) at 0.4 compression ratio for policy training and main evaluation. We further examine compatibility with memory banks produced by other agent memory systems in Section 4.6. We retrieve at most five evidence items per step for both MemPilot and applicable baselines. Since memory items from different systems can vary substantially in length, we directly compare monetary cost and latency rather than memory-item counts. Additional preference settings are explored in Section 4.4. 4.3. Main Results As shown in Table 1, MemPilot spans distinct qualitycost regimes across both models and benchmarks. The results reveal several consistent trends across methods and settings. (1) Text-centric systems achieve low cost largely by avoiding additional multimodal processing and runtime curation, but this often comes with lower answer quality. In comparison, MemPilot-Bal generally achieves stronger overall quality at moderate cost, while MemPilot-Cost reaches similarly low-cost regimes on most datasets. (2) Runtime adaptation does not necessarily translate into controllable trade-offs. Although GAM, AgeMem, and Mem-T adapt memory processing at inference time, they largely expose fixed operating regime rather than explicitly controlling the qualitycost balance. In contrast, MemPilot spans multiple operating points. (3) Multimodal memory processing can be costly without adaptive allocation. MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse often incur substantially higher inference cost without consistently translating that expense into better answer quality. In contrast, MemPilot selectively invokes external curation and achieves stronger performance at much lower cost in most settings, with the same trend extending to MemEye and MemLens. Overall, MemPilot provides controllable qualitycost trade-offs rather than single performance-oriented operating point. MemPilot-Perf prioritizes answer quality, MemPilot-Bal offers balanced operating point, and MemPilot-Cost further reduces resource usage with greater quality sacrifice. In addition to the main baselines, we include LightMem (Fang et al., 2025), BudgetMem (Zhang et al., 2026b), and OmniSimpleMem (Liu et al., 2026b), which explicitly support performanceefficiency trade-offs. For latency, we report representative fixed-inference baselines together with runtimeadaptive methods, since most query-agnostic systems exhibit nearly unchanged inference behavior and collapse to similar single operating points. Performancecost. As shown in Figure 2(a), MemPilot forms stronger frontier across broad cost range and largely envelopes the competing methods. Compared with trade-off-aware baselines such as LightMem, BudgetMem, and OmniSimpleMem, MemPilot reaches higher quality as additional computation is allocated, while also covering competitive low-cost operating points. Most conventional memory systems expose only fixed qualitycost point, highlighting the additional flexibility provided by learned runtime orchestration. Multimodal systems such as MIRIX, M2A, and MemVerse generally incur much higher cost due to visual processing, whereas MemPilot reduces unnecessary multimodal computation through on-demand curation and selective model delegation. Performancelatency. Figure 2(b) shows similarly broad qualitylatency frontier. MemPilot spans lightweight to performance-oriented configurations, whereas most baselines expose only narrow region or single operating point. Even among runtime-adaptive methods, the achievable latency range remains limited. MemVerse achieves competitive quality at relatively low latency, but lacks explicit trade-off control and incurs substantially higher monetary cost in Figure 2(a). This further highlights that cost and latency capture complementary resource constraints. How Does MemPilot Allocate Runtime Computation? To better understand how MemPilot realizes different trade-offs, we analyze its learned runtime curation behavior in Figure 3. Panels (a) and (b) show that as the optimization preference shifts toward lower cost or lower latency, the policy adjusts multiple control dimensions in coordinated manner rather than relying on single knob. Moving from left to right, MemPilot generally reduces the number of policy steps, the frequency of Curate actions, image access, and policy output tokens. At the same time, evidence count also changes adaptively, indicating that the policy does not simply retrieve less information, but learns to reconfigure how memory is accessed and processed under different resource preferences. Panel (c) further shows that model selection is key mechanism behind this adaptation. Under higher-cost settings, MemPilot relies more heavily on stronger VLMs and LLMs, while lower-cost settings shift computation toward cheaper model groups. Together, these results show that MemPilot learns coherent allocation strategy over curation depth, modality access, and routed model capacity, which explains its ability to realize controllable performancecostlatency trade-offs. 4.6. We ablate four key components of MemPilot to examine their contributions to runtime orchestration and policy optimization, with Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. As shown in Table 2, removing LLM/VLM delegation reduces the average Judge score from 37.40 to 14.58, highlighting the importance of adaptive external curation. Removing marginal utility or retrievalinstruction decoupling causes similarly large degradation, demonstrating the value of fine-grained credit assignment and separating evidence retrieval from curation instructions. Objective-wise advantage decoupling is also important for multi-objective training, with its removal reducing the Judge score to 21.94. Although all ablated variants consume less inference cost, their substantial quality losses indicate that simply reducing runtime computation does not yield desirable trade-off. To examine whether MemPilot depends on particular queryagnostic memory construction, we replace its default memory bank with off-the-shelf agent memory banks and evaluate the performancecost frontiers without retraining using Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct as an answer model. Figure 4 reports averages across five benchmarks. The resulting frontiers are clearly separated: the default bank occupies the lower-cost regime, SimpleMem provides an intermediate profile, while A-MEM incurs higher cost but reaches stronger performance. Each memory bank thus induces distinct operating regime, while MemPilot improves performance as additional runtime computation is allocated. This demonstrates compatibility with diverse upstream memory systems while preserving their distinct performancecost characteristics through runtime orchestration. Figure 4 Memory-bank compatibility. Performancecost frontiers with different memory-bank initializations. 5. Conclusion We presented MemPilot, framework for orchestrating on-demand memory curation under controllable performancecostlatency preferences. MemPilot formulates runtime memory adaptation as multi-step decision process, combines query-agnostic memory with raw interaction history, and adaptively delegates curation to heterogeneous LLMs and VLMs. We further introduced resource-aware policy optimization with objective-wise advantage decoupling and prefix-based marginal utility for fine-grained credit assignment. Experiments across multimodal agent-memory benchmarks demonstrate that MemPilot achieves favorable trade-off frontiers while adapting computation to different optimization preferences. We hope this work encourages agent memory systems to move beyond performance-only optimization toward resource-aware runtime adaptation.

Evaluation Details Memory preprocessing and indexing. We serialize each multimodal conversation in chronological order and partition it into approximately 256-token text chunks. Dialogue turns are treated as atomic units: turn is never split across chunks, and its attached images, image identifiers, and captions remain associated with the same chunk. An oversized individual turn is retained as single chunk. For WorldMemArena (Liu et al., 2026a), the memory available to each question is additionally restricted to the cumulative conversation prefix visible at its corresponding checkpoint. We construct separate dense indexes for the raw and compressed memory corpora. Query-agnostic compression is performed independently for chunk text and image captions using LLMLingua-2 (Pan et al., 2024) with default compression rate of 0.4, while memory and image identifiers remain unchanged. Document embeddings are computed offline using Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025c), normalized, stored in float16 format, and reused throughout evaluation. At runtime, only the policy-generated retrieval query is encoded, after which evidence is ranked by embedding similarity. The compressed-memory and raw-memory indexes are searched independently, with at most five retrieved items per curation operation. Image captions participate in textual retrieval, whereas image pixels are made available only when an image-capable external model is selected. Reference answers are never used during preprocessing, indexing, or retrieval. Benchmarks and data splits. Our in-distribution evaluation covers Mem-Gallery (Bei et al., 2026), the lifelong subset of WorldMemArena (Liu et al., 2026a), and both the dyadic and multiparty variants of H2HMem (Zhu et al., 2026). Each dataset is split at the conversation level into 70% training, 10% validation, and 20% test data, ensuring that questions derived from the same conversation never appear in different splits. WorldMemArena is additionally stratified by category and scenario. The 19 MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents source datasets are split independently before their training and validation portions are merged, and their source identities are preserved for dataset-wise reporting. For out-of-distribution evaluation, we use the complete open-answer portion of MemEye (Guo et al., 2026), containing 371 questions across eight scenarios, and the official 32K memory-agent subset of MEMLENS (Ren et al., 2026). MemEyes multiple-choice variant is excluded. MEMLENS answerrefusal questions are removed, leaving 173 of the 195 agent-subset questions. Answer-refusal questions are likewise excluded from Mem-Gallery and H2HMem. For H2HMem, we additionally remove dialogues without usable memory content and Conflict Detection instances whose reference labels cannot satisfy the benchmarks required standalone Yes/No answer format. More Experimental Results B.1. Per-Benchmark Runtime Computation Allocation Figure 5 provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the runtime-allocation analysis in Section 4.5. The overall behavior is consistent across all five benchmarks. As stronger cost or latency preferences 21 MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents are imposed, MemPilot generally reduces policy steps, Curate actions, visual access, and policygeneration tokens, indicating coordinated adaptation across multiple control dimensions. Model routing exhibits an equally consistent shift. High-resource settings rely heavily on larger LLMs and VLMs, whereas tighter cost preferences progressively move curation toward lighter models. At the lowest displayed cost point, all five benchmarks route exclusively to LLMs below 70B. Meanwhile, individual controls such as evidence depth and image access need not change monotonically, showing that MemPilot reallocates computation jointly rather than uniformly shrinking every decision dimension. These results confirm that the aggregate behavior observed in the main text is broadly consistent across datasets while retaining dataset-specific curation patterns. B.2. Per-Benchmark Ablation Results Table 6 provides the per-benchmark breakdown of the ablation study. The full MemPilot configuration consistently achieves the highest Judge score across all five benchmarks. Among the ablations, removing objective-wise advantage decoupling generally preserves the strongest performance, yet still causes clear degradation on every dataset, confirming its role in multi-objective policy optimization. Removing LLM/VLM delegation, marginal utility, or retrievalinstruction decoupling leads to substantially larger drops, with similar trends observed on both in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks. Although all ablations reduce inference cost, the accompanying quality degradation remains pronounced, indicating that the complete design yields more effective qualitycost trade-off rather than merely consuming additional computation. Limitations and Future Work While MemPilot provides flexible runtime memory orchestration, several aspects could be further improved: Privacy-aware delegation. Runtime curation may send retrieved interaction history to external models, which can raise privacy concerns for sensitive memories. Future work could incorporate privacy-aware routing, local processing, or access-control mechanisms while remaining orthogonal to MemPilots core orchestration design. Preference calibration. MemPilot controls trade-offs through predefined optimization preferences. Future work could study more user-friendly ways to map high-level deployment preferences to reward coefficients, making trade-off specification easier across applications. Deployment-aware latency modeling. We use proxy latency estimator during training to avoid instability from transient network and serving fluctuations. Future work could instead optimize directly against measured latency in controlled system-level sandbox with stable networking and serving conditions. E. Broader Impact MemPilot advocates broader shift in agent memory from performance-oriented optimization toward explicit and controllable performancecostlatency trade-offs. In practical deployments, the highestperforming memory configuration is not always the most desirable, as different users and applications may place substantially different values on monetary cost and response latency. This mirrors modern commercial LLM services, which increasingly offer model tiers spanning different capability, cost, and latency profiles (e.g., GPT-5.6-Sol/Terra/Luna), allowing users to choose operating points that best match their needs. We believe agent memory systems should provide similar flexibility rather than committing to single performance-oriented configuration. This becomes particularly relevant for multimodal agents, where accessing and processing visual evidence can introduce substantially different resource demands. More broadly, treating memory curation as adaptive computation allocation may encourage tighter integration between agent memory, model routing, and resourceaware decision making, enabling future long-horizon agents to become more efficient, responsive, and deployment-aware.
